# Multimodal Characterization of Articular Cartilage Degeneration in the Humeral Head Using Raman Spectroscopy, Biomechanics, and Imaging

**Authors:** Mason J. Garcia; Dev R. Mehrotra; Jake Giering; Erik E. Ersland; Alberto Lalli; Giovanni Intermesoli; Shubham Laiwala; Olaia Rackauskas; Mario Keko; Prateek Misra; Brian D. Snyder; Joseph P. DeAngelis; Umile Giuseppe Longo; Michael B. Albro; Arun J. Ramappa; Ara Nazarian

**Affiliations:** 1 Musculoskeletal Translational Innovation Initiative, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 2 Boston University, Mechanical Engineering Department, Boston, MA, USA | 3 Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Campus Bio-Medico, Roma, Italy | 4 Department of Medicine and Surgery, Research Unit of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, Università Campus Bio-Medico di Roma, Roma, Italy | 5 Boston University, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Boston, MA, USA | 6 Carl J. Shapiro Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 7 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Yerevan State Medical University, Yerevan, Armenia

## Abstract

This study evaluated articular cartilage degeneration in the humeral head using a multimodal approach integrating Raman spectroscopy, mechanical testing, biochemical analysis, and micro-computed tomography (μCT). The goal was to identify sensitive biomarkers of early matrix-level degeneration that precede overt radiographic changes in glenohumeral osteoarthritis (OA).

Eleven humeral heads were collected from cadaveric shoulders and stratified by the presence of a focal chondral defect and rotator cuff (RC) tear status, yielding four specimens without visual cartilage degeneration (controls) and seven samples (3 RC + OA, 4 OA Only) with visual defects. Raman spectroscopy was used to non-destructively quantify the contents of cartilage glycosaminoglycan (GAG), collagen (COL), and water (H2O). Tissue stiffness was assessed via indentation mechanical testing, and biochemical composition was assessed via DMMB (GAG) and OHP (COL) assays and gravimetric H2O content. μCT imaging quantified trabecular bone architecture.

Cartilage from degenerated regions exhibited decreased mechanical stiffness with a corresponding reduction in GAG and an increase in tissue hydration. Raman-derived GAGscore accounted for 68% of the variation in indentation modulus and outperformed conventional Outerbridge grading in identifying tissue with compromised mechanical function. μCT revealed thinning of subchondral trabeculae in areas adjacent to cartilage degeneration.

Cartilage degeneration in the glenohumeral joint is characterized by extracellular matrix (ECM) loss, increased hydration, compromised mechanical function, and alterations to the trabecular structure. Raman spectroscopy enabled the production of non-destructive spatial maps of tissue ECM composition, highlighting the progressive OA-associated changes in specimens with and without focal defects.

## Introduction

Glenohumeral osteoarthritis (OA) leads to significant pain, discomfort, and disability. It has been reported that radiographical findings of glenohumeral OA are as high as 16–20% in the middle-aged and older adult populations1. Among patients with non-traumatic shoulder pain, glenohumeral OA is the second most common cause of shoulder pain, behind rotator cuff tears2. Furthermore, Studies have reported that 7–26% of patients with RC tears also present with concurrent OA3, 4. However, the exact pathogenesis of this disease remains largely unknown, with risk factors including obesity, sedentary lifestyle, increasing age, genetics, diet, previous joint injury, and abnormal joint loading conditions5. With an increasingly aging population, the impact of and potential treatment courses for OA have become increasingly significant, particularly with respect to the progressive deterioration of cartilage and bone. The degenerative OA changes in the hip and knee are well documented, as a greater proportion of patients experience hip and knee OA than shoulder OA6–8. However, the shoulder is the third most common large joint to be affected by OA9. Despite this, there is a lack of understanding and characterization of glenohumeral OA, with only a few studies evaluating degenerative changes within the join10–12.

Compositionally, the extracellular matrix (ECM) of the articular cartilage is largely comprised of a collagen (COL) network, which supports its structure and tensile properties, and a negatively charged glycosaminoglycan (GAG) matrix, which provides compressive strength and retains interstitial water (H2O)13, 14. These ECM constituents give rise to the capability of articular cartilage in resisting compressive and shear loads, while maintaining low-friction joint locomotion15, 16. Degeneration of these constituents can manifest as chondral lesions, which, if left untreated, progress until bone-on-bone contact occurs. Studies have shown that glenohumeral OA results in a loss of cartilage thicknes11 and increased histological scorin10, 12, indicating structural and compositional changes. However, these studies were limited to end-stage glenohumeral OA and did not examine the specific mechanical or compositional changes in the regions where defects are present. Thus, it remains unclear whether osteoarthritis progression in the non-weight-bearing glenohumeral joint exhibits patterns of cartilage degeneration and phenotypic change comparable to those observed in weight-bearing joints such as the hip and knee.

Glenohumeral OA often progresses insidiously, likely with early changes in cartilage composition preceding macroscopic defects or joint space narrowing. In this study, tissue was harvested from cadaveric shoulders exhibiting focal chondral defects and similar-matched controls. This study focuses on the degenerative changes experienced by cartilage and trabecular bone, which may be relevant for early intervention and detection of OA, prior to the end-stage of the disease, where clinical intervention typically involves joint replacement. The objective is to evaluate compositional and mechanical changes associated with cartilage degeneration in cadaveric humeral head specimens exhibiting focal chondral defects, both with and without RC tears. Cartilage composition will be assessed using Raman spectroscopy, a non-invasive technique that utilizes inelastic light scattering to reflect tissue molecular bond vibrational modes, generating an “optical fingerprint” of tissue composition17. An intra-articular-compatible Raman probe will be used to enable non-destructive assessment of cartilage18–20. Through a multivariate spectral decomposition analysis, ECM-specific optical biomarkers reflecting cartilage composition are extracted18–20. These Raman-based measurements will be complemented by biochemical analysis, mechanical testing, and micro-computed tomography (μCT) to comprehensively assess changes in cartilage composition and mechanical integrity, as well as alterations in subchondral bone structure associated with glenohumeral OA. First, hypothesize that degenerative changes in the humeral head due to OA result in measurable alterations in extracellular matrix composition and mechanical stiffness as well as changes to the trabecular bone architecture. Second, we hypothesize that OA + RC will have differing regions of degeneration but similar changes to composition due to the shifting of the humeral head as a result of RC tear.

## Methods

### Tissue Samples

The humeral heads from eleven fresh frozen disarticulated cadaveric shoulders (6 Male/5 Female) with a mean age of 61 ± 4 years old were used in this study (Medcure, Providence, RI, USA). The specimens were then divided into two groups based on visual macroanalysis of the humeral head cartilage. All specimens were obtained in this age range to ensure both groups were of similar age, and we were not comparing young, healthy samples to older degenerated samples. Specimens with no visual signs of cartilage degeneration were designated to the intact control group (N = 4; mean age 62 ± 3) and specimens with visual focal defects to the cartilage were designated to the defect group (N = 7; mean age 60 ± 4). Sites with full cartilage erosion (exposed subchondral bone) were not subjected to analysis. Of the humeral heads that had evidence of degeneration, 3 came from specimens where there was a concurrent rotator cuff tear identified upon dissection by inspection of the supraspinatus tendon. The humeral heads were then sectioned using a rectangular grid pattern to create square osteochondral blocks using a fine-tooth handsaw (N = 7–10 blocks/humeral head)19. Overall, this yielded 90 osteochondral samples across all donors for subsequent testing. Specimens that had no signs of macro-degeneration were assigned to the intact group (n = 66 osteochondral specimens) and those with visual focal defects were assigned to the defect group (n = 24 osteochondral specimens). Tissue samples were subjected to Raman spectroscopy, mechanical indentation, biochemical analysis (GAG, COL, H2O content), μCT imaging, histology, and Outerbridge visual grading. All specimens were kept hydrated in 1× PBS and stored at −20 °C.

### Raman Spectroscopy

The Raman instrumentation is comprised of a custom Raman probe, with a threaded, hollow needle tip possessing a distal mounted ∅2mm diameter sapphire ball lens (InPhotonics, Norwood, MA, USA), coupled to an NIR diode laser (ex = 785 nm; 125 mW output; IPS) and a spectrometer (Eagle Raman-S, Ibsen Photonics, Farum, Denmark) equipped with a near infrared (NIR) optimized charge coupled device (Ivac, Andor, Belfast, Northern Ireland) Andor)19. The distal end of this needle probe contains a ∅2mm sapphire ball lens, with the focal distance being close to zero requiring direct contact with the cartilage surface for sufficient spectral acquisition. For Raman spectral acquisitions, the probe tip was positioned perpendicular to the articular surface of each osteochondral explant (N = 90; N = 66 Intact, N = 24 Defect), and spectra were acquired using a 30s integration time. Following subtraction of the probe background, a 3rd order polynomial baseline correction and subsequent area-under-curve normalization were applied to the 800–1800 cm−1 spectral “fingerprint” region. The resulting “fingerprint” spectrum was decomposed using the following multivariate regression model20: Cartilage spectra = G A G score * GAG ref + COL score * COL ref + H 2 O score * H 2 O ref + Bone score * Bone ref

The derived regression coefficients ( GAG score , COL score , H 2 O score , Bone Score ) reflect the relative contribution of each individual constituent to the overall composite spectrum, thereby providing a non-destructive assessment of individual osteochondral explant composition (Figure 1). GAGREF, CollagenREF, H2OREF, and BoneREF are reference spectra measured from purified chemicals of each constituent (Figure 1C): GAGREF= chondroitin sulfate [bovine cartilage; C6737 Sigma]; CollagenREF= type-II collagen [chicken sternal cartilage; C9301 Sigma]; H2OREF= PBS; BoneREF= Mature bovine subchondral bone.

### Mechanical Testing

Each osteochondral explant (N = 90) was subject to indentation testing at the center of the cartilage layer using a custom mechanical testing machine (CellScale Biomaterials, Waterloo, ON, Canada). A ∅2mm diameter spherical indenter was used to apply a 100 μm tissue displacement at a loading rate of 5 μm/s to obtain the cartilage force-displacement response. The compressive modulus was then obtained assuming Hertzian contact theory for the loading curve21.

### Outerbridge Scoring

A visual assessment of the cartilage breakdown was performed for all specimens with a visual defect (N = 24) and a random subset of visually intact specimens (N = 10) to assess the relationship between clinical assessments of cartilage and mechanical function. A single experienced orthopaedic shoulder surgeon graded the specimens according to the Outerbridge classification system22. The Outerbridge classification was chosen because it represents the current convention for assessing cartilage health during arthroscopic procedures and has previously been used to assess shoulder joint articular cartilage23.

### Biochemical Analysis

A central ∅4mm chondral sub-punch was collected from the center of each osteochondral explant (N = 76; N = 56 Intact, N = 19 Defect), co-localized with the region subjected to mechanical and Raman assessments. Upon separation of the cartilage from the bone, the wet weight of the cartilage was recorded. Following lyophilization, the tissue dry weight was measured, providing the gravimetric water content. Subsequently, the tissue was digested with proteinase K and analyzed for GAG and collagen content using 1,9-dimethylmethylene blue (DMMB) and orthohydroxyproline (OHP) assays, respectively.

### Histological Evaluation

A random subset of degenerated (N = 3) and intact (N = 3) osteochondral specimens was fixed in formalin, embedded in paraffin, sectioned, and stained with safranin-O/fast green to assess the presence of GAG. Slides were imaged with a 20× objective on a standard bright-field microscope to provide representative images of intact and degenerated tissue (Figure 3A and 3 B).

### Micro-computed Tomography

Osteochondral specimens were scanned (N = 23 degenerated, N = 19 intact controls from defect-free humeral heads) (μCT40, SCANCO Medical, Brütisellen, Switzerland) under the following conditions: The x-ray tube was operated at 70 kVp, an intensity of 114 mA and an integration time of 300 ms. This resulted in an isotropic voxel size of 15μm. The bone density and micro-architectural indices (Bone Mineral Density (BMD, mgHA/cm3 ), Bone Volume Fraction (BV/TV, mm3/mm3), Trabecular Thickness (Tb.Th, mm), and Connectivity Density (Conn.D, 1/mm3) were calculated along the central 20 slices of each specimen, where a 2mm volume of interest was manually drawn directly adjacent to the cartilage layer, allowing for the evaluation of changes in trabecular bone.

### Statistical Analysis

All data is presented as median (interquartile range). We used the proc mixed from the SAS software, version 9.4 for the Windows System to implement a mixed model for testing the differences in the selected “compositional/mechanical/ μCT variables” (i.e., Modulus, GAG, COL, H2O, BMD, BV/TV, Conn.D, Tb.Th) by the presence of “damage” (i.e., Intact or Defect; RCT or RCT + OA) in the “cartilage sample” (i.e., each specimen). We used a linear mixed-effects model with random intercepts to address multiple measurements from the same subject. Spearman’s rank test was used to determine the correlation between Outerbridge grade and compressive modulus. A nonlinear (2nd order polynomial) regression was performed to determine the extent to which variation in the Raman GAGscore accounted for the variation in compressive modulus as assessed by the coefficient of determination (adjusted R2). Two-tailed p-values < 0.05 were considered significant. The specimens obtained were based on what was available, and no a priori sample size or power calculations was performed.

## Results

### Spatial Maps of Humeral Head Degeneration from Raman Spectroscopy

Spatial maps of the cartilage mechanical function and Raman-derived biomarkers for specimens with increasing levels of degeneration are shown in Figure 2 to illustrate the compositional and mechanical changes that occur as cartilage degenerates. Shown are two intact controls, one specimen with a small defect (< 0.5 cm2) and one specimen with a larger defect (> 1.5 cm2), to highlight the changes in the degenerated regions as the focal defect increases in size. Here we see the progression from an intact control with seemingly uniform mechanical and compositional properties, to the complete loss of mechanics and composition when the defect comprises most of the humeral head.

### Cartilage Mechanical Health

Cartilage degeneration resulted in a significant decrease in mechanical function, as evidenced by a reduction in the compressive modulus. The osteochondral specimens with focal defects had a lower elastic modulus than the intact group (Table 1 & Figure 3A). Clinically, cartilage health can be assessed during arthroscopic procedures, where the degree of degeneration can be graded on the Outerbridge scale (0-IV). Therefore, we compared the relationship between Outerbridge grade and the elastic modulus to assess if the gold standard for cartilage degeneration can explain mechanical degradation. In the osteochondral specimens with defects and 10 randomly chosen visually intact specimens (Outerbridge Grade 0). No correlation (p = 0.13) between the elastic modulus and Outerbridge classification (Figure 3B) was found in this subset of specimens.

### Histological Assessment of Cartilage

The three intact (Figure 3C) and defective (Figure 3D) specimens were qualitatively evaluated to verify the presence/absence of GAG. In intact samples, we observe uniform cartilage thickness and GAG in the deep zone. Although one sample (Figure 3C–3) appears to have a loss of GAG, which could be attributed to early degenerative changes, where cartilage thinning has not yet occurred. Furthermore, there is a lack of GAG in the superficial layer, which may be attributed to the advanced age of these specimens, as they are likely to have undergone degeneration due to aging26. Similarly, the advanced age of these specimens may explain the absence of a GAG signal in the cartilage's superficial region. In the defect samples, there is heterogeneity in the cartilage thickness, where there is a loss of GAG signal directly under the site of cartilage thinning (Figure 3D).

### Comparison of Cartilage Degeneration to Intact Controls

Regions containing focal defects exhibited significant compositional changes relative to intact controls, as measured by both Raman spectroscopy and biochemical analysis (Table 1 and Figure 4). Raman spectroscopy and biochemical analysis revealed a significant reduction in GAG levels between intact and focal-defect samples. Biochemical analysis also revealed a significant increase in tissue hydration. While the Raman-derived H2O and COL did not reach significance between the defect and controls, there was a slight decrease in COL and an increase in H2O. Raman-derived biomarkers were also found to have positive correlations to their corresponding biochemical assays (GAGscore vs GAG content, R2 = 0.54, p < 0.001; COLscore vs. COL content, R2 = 0.19, p = 0.016; H2Oscore vs H2O content, R2 =0.19, p < 0.001).

### Correlation between Raman-derived biomarkers and mechanical function

Overall, intact cartilage had a higher compressive modulus than regions with focal lesions. As a result of degeneration, there was a loss of GAG within the cartilage, which was seen in both the GAGscore and GAG content. A 2nd-order polynomial fit using the Raman-derived GAGscore captured 68% of the variability in the compressive modulus of the osteochondral specimens (Figure 5), indicating that stiffer tissue was associated with higher GAGscore (adjusted R2 = 0.68, p < 0.001).

### Bone microarchitecture

μCT imaging revealed changes to the underlying trabecular structure of the specimens with a defect (Table 1 and Figure 6). There was a significant reduction in BV/TV (p = 0.011). Yet, there were no statistically significant differences in BMD, Conn.D, or Tb.Th.

### Comparison of Degeneration with RC Injury

To assess if RC injury results in differences in the compositional and mechanical changes of cartilage, we compared the Raman-derived biomarkers and compressive modulus of the osteochondral samples with macroscopic damage (focal defects) from humeral heads with RC tears versus those without RC tears (Figure 7). This resulted in n = 10 osteochondral specimens in the RC tear + OA groups and n = 14 osteochondral specimens in the OA only group. Overall, no statistically significant differences in the compositional or mechanical properties between specimens with RCT + OA versus OA (Table 2 and Figures 7A–D) were seen. No statistically significant differences were found between the RCT + OA group compared to the OA only group for BV/TV, BMD, Conn.D, or Tb.Th.

Cartilage degeneration was generally seen in the central portion of the humeral head (Figure 7), consistent with previous studies evaluating end-stage OA10, 11. However, different phenotypes of OA may exist due to concurrent pathology, such as RC arthropathy. Three of the humeral heads with cartilage degeneration also had RC tears; therefore, we plotted the location of degeneration to qualitatively identify changes in the wear pattern. Cartilage degeneration was located centrally when there was no RC tear (Figure 7G); however, the specimens with a RC tear (n = 3) exhibited an inferior shift in the degeneration sites (Figure 7H).

## Discussion

Our study directly evaluates the degenerative alterations in glenohumeral OA. We observed a significant reduction in glycosaminoglycan (GAG) content, a critical component of the extracellular matrix (ECM), as well as elevated water content (H2O), all measured via biochemical and Raman-derived scores. These findings align with established OA models where early cartilage degeneration is associated with GAG depletion, ECM swelling (increased hydration), and eventual disruption of the collagen network7. This degradation cascade reduces stiffness and increases permeability, impairing the tissue’s capacity to resist compressive forces27.

Numerous studies have assessed the thickness of humeral head articular cartilage28–31, but these are largely limited to non-degenerated samples, with only one study examining the native mechanical properties31. Although cartilage is generally thickest centrally and thinnest peripherally28, compressive properties do not appear to differ regionally31. While cartilage thinning is a hallmark of OA, it offers limited insight into underlying compositional and mechanical changes. Raman spectroscopy enables non-destructive evaluation of tissue composition and distinguishes between intact and degenerated cartilage samples. We found that compositional degeneration, as measured by Raman spectroscopy, decreases the tissue’s resistance to compression, with the Raman-derived GAGscore accounting for 68% of the variation in the compressive modulus. GAGscore offers a useful metric to evaluate cartilage mechanical function and can potentially distinguish regions where cartilage visually appears healthy but is functionally deficient. Thus, Raman spectroscopy provides a sensitive, non-destructive approach to detect early, matrix-level degeneration that precedes visible thinning, offering valuable insight into cartilage pathology and a potential tool for early OA detection in the shoulder.

While our study demonstrates that glenohumeral osteoarthritis (OA) involves cartilage degeneration leading to compositional loss and reduced mechanical function, it is important to recognize OA as a whole-joint disease that also affects subchondral bone architecture32. Prior studies have reported central thickening of the subchondral bone plate in humeral heads, indicative of sclerosis10, 11, though these analyses were limited to specimens from patients with end-stage OA. Using μCT imaging, we evaluated trabecular bone beneath focal cartilage defects and found structural deterioration, including a significant reduction in BV/TV compared to intact controls. These findings align with previous work, showing trabecular deterioration is an early feature of OA33. The absence of increased BMD, a hallmark of late-stage OA-associated sclerosis33, suggests that the cadaveric samples may reflect early-stage OA. Our results reinforce the notion that cartilage degeneration in glenohumeral OA occurs alongside early, yet measurable, alterations in subchondral bone structure, highlighting the joint-wide nature of the disease.

This study demonstrates that cartilage degeneration in the glenohumeral joint mirrors the patterns observed in weight-bearing joints such as the hip and knee. In these joints, OA is characterized by ECM degradation, including a loss of GAG, COL, and increased tissue hydration34–36. While abnormal mechanical loading has been implicated in initiating degeneration through structural and functional alterations in cartilage and bone37, OA is now recognized as a multifactorial disease, with inflammation38 and metabolic dysregulation51 also contributing significantly. Though the shoulder is not subjected to the same loading as weight-bearing joints, it is not immune to these biological mechanisms. Disruption in the RC force balance, particularly due to RC tears, can result in eccentric loading of the glenohumeral joint39, 40, increasing cartilage stress and potentially triggering damage. This altered biomechanics, coupled with an inflammatory response, may explain why shoulder OA shares phenotypic similarities with weight-bearing joint degeneration. This study found that cartilage degeneration occurs predominantly in the central region of the humeral head, consistent with previous studies evaluating end-stage shoulder O10–12. RC tears alter the mechanical environment of the glenohumeral joint, and as tears progress, the force couples acting across the glenohumeral joint become unbalanced, which results in superior migration of the humeral head41–43. As a result of the altered mechanical environment, degenerative changes to the joint may occur, often referred to as RC arthropathy44–46. The superior migration of the humeral head leads to abnormal wear conditions of the humeral head, as the inferior region of the humeral head meets the glenoid. Although our sample size of specimens with RC tears and cartilage degeneration is small, this may explain why we observe an apparent inferior shift in the location of degeneration in joints with RC tears.

Understanding osteoarthritis (OA) development in the glenohumeral joint is crucial, as age, overuse, and co-existing injuries, such as rotator cuff (RC) tears, can damage the humeral head articular cartilage47. Even after successful RC repair, OA can develop in 12–29% of patients within 10 years47, despite evidence that RC repair helps restore native joint loading48. This suggests biomechanical alterations may initiate cartilage degeneration before macroscopic signs appear. Our study demonstrates that Raman spectroscopy can non-destructively assess cartilage composition, building on prior findings linking composition to functio19, 20, 49. In the future, Raman spectroscopy may offer the potential for in-vivo measurements of cartilage health50, which could help identify patients at risk of developing OA after RC repair. Notably, Raman-derived assessments have the ability to assess the compositional and mechanical deficits in cartilage that appear visually intact19, which Outerbridge grading, the current clinical gold standard, failed to detect.

This study should be interpreted in light of its limitations. The sample size was limited, especially in subgroups with cartilage degeneration and concurrent RC tears, necessitating pooling all degenerated samples. This reflects the challenge of acquiring such specimens. Furthermore, within our control group, it is likely that they do not represent true “healthy” levels of ECM composition and mechanical function, which may be lost due to aging26, but precede macroscopic damage. Another explanation as to why the GAG may seem lower compared to previous studies in the knee19, 20, is that the shoulder is non-weight bearing and sees smaller compressive forces compared to the knee, making it plausible that GH cartilage is softer and naturally has less GAG. While cadaveric samples offer important insights into tissue composition and mechanics, they may not fully represent in vivo behavior or disease progression, as assessments were limited to static measurements. The absence of end-stage OA samples also restricted comparisons and may have prevented the observation of advanced changes, such as subchondral sclerosis, or the ability to definitively say that these samples represent early OA. Nevertheless, despite these constraints, the study provides important new insights into previously uncharacterized early degenerative changes in cartilage and bone within the glenohumeral joint.

This study presents the first comprehensive multimodal analysis of articular cartilage degeneration in the humeral head using Raman spectroscopy, mechanical testing, biochemical assays, and μCT imaging to characterize early osteoarthritic changes. Subchondral bone thinning without sclerosis indicates early glenohumeral OA, aligning with changes seen in weight-bearing joints. We found that focal degeneration is associated with consistent extracellular matrix changes and reduced stiffness. Raman-derived biomarkers were highly correlated to cartilage mechanical properties and outperformed Outerbridge grading in detecting early degeneration.
